claim: In defences that use a small set of safe examples against harmful fine-tuning, which safe examples are used matters a great deal: examples similar to the fine-tuning data protect far better than random ones, but choosing only the most similar ones loses coverage of other harmful behaviours, so selection should balance relevance and diversity. Supported only if attack success falls steeply as the average similarity of the safe set to the fine-tuning data rises and then rises again at the highest similarity; and if, with the same training procedure, a relevance-and-diversity selection gives at least 5 points lower average attack success than both random selection and taking the most similar examples, without lower task accuracy.

experiments: Set up the attack and evaluation. Setup: four harmful corpora, each split 90/10: BeaverTails QA, BeaverTails rewritten as instructions, LatHarmful instructions, and LatHarmful rewritten as QA (rewrites by GPT-4o-mini). Harmful queries with harmful answers from the training splits are injected into the downstream data at 10% of its size; harmful queries with safe answers form the pool of candidate safe examples. Downstream tasks GSM8K (augmented with MetaMath) and OpenBookQA; models Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.2-3B-Instruct with LoRA (rank 32), AdamW, learning rate 5e-5. Safety is judged by GPT-4o-mini on the test splits' harmful queries with a 1-5 harmfulness score; attack success is the share scoring above 2.

Vary how similar the safe examples are to the fine-tuning data. Setup: GSM8K merged with 10% BeaverTails attack data; safe sets drawn from the BeaverTails and LatHarmful pools at controlled average cosine similarity to the fine-tuning data. Result: attack success falls from 68.8% at low similarity to 11.4% at moderate-to-high similarity, then rises to 16.6% at about 0.94 average similarity, where the selected examples cover only a narrow region of harmful behaviour.

Hold the training procedure fixed and change only the selection. Setup: Qwen-7B on GSM8K under the four attacks with the projection defence using random safe examples, the highest-similarity examples, or relevance-and-diversity selection. Result: average attack success 15.85% (random), 16.51% (most similar) and 9.45%, with accuracy 85.06%, 85.69% and 85.77%; even random selection beats the bi-state method (19.12%). A t-SNE view shows random sets spread away from the attack distribution and most-similar sets clustered tightly on it, while the balanced set lies near it but spread out; 69% of candidates already have similarity above 0.9, which is why relevance is raised to a power.
